pl-l3d33c3-d1e115.summary: Quotes Augustine raising the question whether these virtues, which begin to be in the mind and so are not identical with it, cease to be when they have led to eternal things.

pl-l3d33c3-d1e120.summary: Continues the quotation: some have thought they will cease, and of prudence, fortitude, and temperance this seems to say something.
claims: Some hold that prudence, fortitude, and temperance will cease.

pl-l3d33c3-d1e124.summary: Continues: justice is immortal and will be perfected rather than cease in beatitude, when we live in contemplation of the divine nature, the best and most lovable, to which it belongs to justice to be subject. So justice will not cease but be so great it cannot be greater.
claims: Justice is immortal and will be perfected in beatitude.
Justice consists in subjection to God.

pl-l3d33c3-d1e129.summary: Continues: perhaps the other three will also be in that happiness: prudence without danger of error, fortitude without trouble, temperance without opposition of lust; prudence will consist in preferring or equating no good to God, fortitude in clinging to him firmly, temperance in delighting in no harmful defect.
claims: Prudence, fortitude, and temperance may remain in beatitude in a new form.

pl-l3d33c3-d1e133.summary: Concludes the quotation: what justice, prudence, fortitude, and temperance now do will not be there, where there is no evil. These works, necessary for this mortal life, like faith to which they are referred, will be past.
claims: The present works of the virtues will cease in the homeland.

pl-l3d33c3-d1e139.summary: Draws out that Augustine openly says these virtues will exist in the future but with other uses than now.
claims: The cardinal virtues will remain in the future with other uses.

pl-l3d33c3-d1e145.summary: Adds that Bede agrees, interpreting the pillars before the veil in Exodus as the heavenly powers distinguished by the four virtues, kept differently in heaven by angels and souls than here by the faithful, and assigning their uses in the present and future state after Augustine.
claims: Bede agrees that the virtues are kept differently in heaven.

pl-l3d33c3.summary: Asks, with Augustine, whether the cardinal virtues cease when they have led to eternal things. Some think they cease, which seems plausible for prudence, fortitude, and temperance; but justice is immortal and will be perfected in beatitude, as subjection to God. Perhaps the other three will also remain: prudence without danger of error, fortitude without trouble, temperance without struggle against lust, so that prudence prefers no good to God, fortitude cleaves to him, and temperance delights in no harmful defect. Their present works, helping the wretched and the rest, will not be there, as faith will be past. Lombard concludes that Augustine teaches the virtues will remain with other uses, and Bede agrees.
claims: Justice is immortal and will be perfected in beatitude.
Prudence, fortitude, and temperance will also remain, with other uses.
The present works of the cardinal virtues will cease in the homeland.
The virtues are kept in heaven differently than here.
